noticias.titulo: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
noticias.resumen: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
noticias.texto:
'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
- Published
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.
Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.
The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.
"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."
The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line
Related topics
  - Published23 September

noticias.titulo: Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
noticias.resumen: Hundreds of thousands of people were without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
noticias.texto:
Severe Thanksgiving storms leave roads flooded and trees fallen
Both US coasts have been battered by severe Thanksgiving storms, leaving behind flooded roads, fallen trees, and widespread power outages for hundreds of thousands of people.
Although the weather is expected to improve, hundreds of flights remain delayed or cancelled on Friday.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the east Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

noticias.titulo: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
noticias.resumen: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
noticias.texto:
Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
- Published
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.
"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."
Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.
Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.
"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".
"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.
"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.
"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."
The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.
He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."
* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

noticias.titulo: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
noticias.resumen: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
noticias.texto:
A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
- Published
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.
The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.
The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.
And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable â and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Barred from jobs
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.
This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.
Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (Â£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.
But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.
Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?
Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.
The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian LundstrÃ¶m, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.
LundstrÃ¶m says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism SkÃ¥ne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.
Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
LundstrÃ¶m says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
'I was stuck'
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, LundstrÃ¶m explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.
Before opening the clinic, LundstrÃ¶m conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.
During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to LundstrÃ¶m, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.
During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.
But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.
Fears about stigma
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.
"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister VÃ¤sternorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.
Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of RiksfÃ¶rbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.
He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
'Magic spell'
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says LundstrÃ¶m, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.
Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.
Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.
The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.
"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.
Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.
She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.
"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

noticias.titulo: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
noticias.resumen: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
noticias.texto:
The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
- Published
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.
Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi â the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.
Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.
How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.
For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name â Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father â Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.
Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.
Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.
During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.
"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.
Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.
Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled â a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."
No one asked for their money back.
But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 â the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.
Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

noticias.titulo: Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' who become an online meme
noticias.resumen: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.
noticias.texto:
Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' who become an online meme
- Published
For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo â the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.
He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.
"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.
"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

noticias.titulo: Parts of US clean up after Thanksgiving storm lashes East Coast
noticias.resumen: Power is being slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers following a round of heavy wind, rain and snow.
noticias.texto:
Parts of US clean up after Thanksgiving storm lashes East Coast
Power is being slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers following a round of heavy wind, rain and snow.
Heavy rain and flooding have begun to ease along the US East Coast as power is being slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers following a round of holiday storms.
The storms disrupted travel and downed trees and power lines, leading to water rescues in multiple states, from New York to Virginia.
In New York City, preparations were under way for the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.
The parade, an annual spectacle usually held on Thanksgiving Day, sees brightly coloured balloons travel through the heart of Manhattan. The festivities also kick off the holiday shopping season for the US.
The same balloons and floats, and most of the original celebrities, are still set to take part, organisers said.
Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.
While conditions are expected to improve across the entire eastern US, the National Weather Service warned that “this huge system will take some time to weaken”.
The low-pressure system that brought the storm to the East Coast, the service added, would continue to slowly exit to the northeast, “bringing lingering showers and isolated freezing precipitation through Saturday”.
Coastal flood warnings were also issued in several states from New Jersey to Virginia.
Power restored, travel disruptions ease
The number of power outages, which peaked on Thursday at more than 900,000, fell to 264,000 by Friday evening as crews worked to restore electricity, according to poweroutage.us.
Pennsylvania had the most, followed by Missouri.
Some flight disruptions also lingered on Friday, with about 1,600 delays and more than 500 cancellations, according to the tracking service FlightAware.
In the southern US, part of Tennessee was under a winter storm warning for up to 2.5cm (one inch) of snow on Friday, after rain turned into light snow on Thanksgiving.
In the Midwest, conditions were calmer than they were the previous day, when as much as 38cm (15 inches) of snow fell in eastern Missouri.
The weather service said heavy snow was still expected in parts of Montana and Wyoming, however.
Along the Pacific coast, waves driven by high tides caused flooding and continued to affect train services. Record tides along the California coast prompted evacuations from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.

noticias.titulo: Hunted beyond borders: Allegations of Tanzanian repression in Kenya
noticias.resumen: The case of a missing activist raises fears for the safety of Tanzanian dissidents.
noticias.texto:
Hunted beyond borders: Allegations of Tanzanian repression in Kenya
The case of a missing activist raises fears for the safety of Tanzanian dissidents.
Nairobi, Kenya – On October 25, 2026, Tanzanian opposition activist Twaha Salim Mwaipaya was travelling in a taxi to visit friends in Kamulu, in Kenya’s Machakos County, when three vehicles intercepted it.
According to the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), unidentified individuals forcibly removed him from the taxi and took him away. His whereabouts remain unknown.
Amnesty International reported that the vehicles included a Toyota Land Cruiser Hardtop. The organisation called on Kenyan authorities to establish Mwaipaya’s whereabouts, guarantee his safety and investigate the circumstances of his disappearance.
The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) subsequently described the incident as an enforced disappearance and called for an independent investigation, including into possible cross-border involvement.
The identities of those responsible have not been established, and it remains unclear who ordered the abduction.
Mwaipaya, a former youth organiser of Tanzania’s opposition party Chadema, had fled to Kenya in 2025, citing threats to his safety.
On November 3, Kenya’s inspector general of police, Douglas Kanja, appeared before the High Court to explain the activist’s whereabouts. He denied that Kenyan police had arrested or detained Mwaipaya.
“We do not have him in our custody,” Kanja told the court, adding that investigations were ongoing. He acknowledged that Mwaipaya’s relatives had reported him missing at a police station in the Ruai area.
Kanja also said he had consulted other security agencies but had received no information confirming that Mwaipaya had been transferred to Tanzania.
The case returned to the High Court on November 23. Judge Alexander Muteti summoned Mohamed Amin, head of the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), to provide an update on the investigation into Mwaipaya’s disappearance.
The judge said Amin’s appearance was necessary because the inspector general had placed the investigation within the DCI’s mandate. The court declined to summon Deputy Inspector General of Police Eliud Lagat, ruling that his testimony would not add significant value to the proceedings. Amin was ordered to appear on a date to be determined by the court.
Tanzania’s high commissioner to Kenya, Bernard Kibesse, told news outlet The Citizen on October 26 that the embassy was following up on the disappearance but had not received an official report.
Mwaipaya’s disappearance recalls the January 2025 abduction of Tanzanian activist and government critic Maria Sarungi Tsehai in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi. Unidentified men forced her into a vehicle before releasing her several hours later following public pressure and intervention by human rights defenders, according to reports at the time by Amnesty International Kenya and other organisations.
Sarungi believes her abductors intended to take her across the border into Tanzania.
“In 60-90 minutes, they would have reached the border and crossed with me, and I would have disappeared for good like hundreds of Tanzanians who have disappeared in such manner in Tanzania under Samia Suluhu,” she told Al Jazeera.
She said some of the men appeared to be Kenyan, while another appeared Tanzanian based on his Kiswahili. She alleged that a Tanzanian national directed the operation. The identities of her abductors and who organised the operation have not been independently established.
The incidents have renewed concerns about the safety of Tanzanian dissidents in Kenya and allegations of transnational repression.
In May 2026, President Samia Suluhu Hassan made remarks about dealing with antigovernment protesters that drew criticism.
Speaking alongside Kenyan President William Ruto at State House in Dar es Salaam on May 4, Hassan said protesters should be flogged with canes if they crossed into either country, The Standard reported.
The leaders were attending a joint press briefing following the signing of eight bilateral agreements.
“I have told President William Ruto we must stand firm against those who lack discipline. We should not choose between Tanzanians or Kenyans. If they come to me, I flog them with canes; if they come to you, you flog them with canes, so that they behave,” Hassan said, according to The Standard’s May 5 report.
Former Kenyan Chief Justice David Maraga condemned the comments, describing them as abhorrent. No evidence has emerged linking the remarks to either abduction.
History of repression
Political repression in Tanzania predates Hassan’s presidency. Under her predecessor, John Magufuli, human rights organisations documented restrictions on political freedoms, intimidation of opposition figures and attacks on government critics.
In September 2017, opposition leader Tundu Lissu survived an assassination attempt in Dodoma, the capital of Tanzania, during which he was shot 16 times by unidentified men. He received treatment in Nairobi before continuing his recovery in Belgium. The attack remains unresolved.
Hassan initially raised hopes of political reform after taking office in 2021, easing restrictions on political rallies and allowing some politicians who had fled the country to return.
However, human rights organisations subsequently documented renewed restrictions on opposition activity, arbitrary arrests and intimidation of critics. The African Union’s 2025 election observation mission also noted that the political opening following her accession had been short-lived.
Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. On November 6, 2026, a Tanzanian court acquitted him of treason but convicted him of incitement, sentencing him to four years in prison.
The Reuters news agency reported that the charges arose from remarks prosecutors said urged supporters to disrupt the election. Lissu denied wrongdoing.
The treatment of critics has also affected activists from neighbouring countries.
In May 2025, Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan human rights defender Agather Atuhaire travelled to Dar-es-Salaam to observe Lissu’s treason proceedings. They were arrested on May 19 and subsequently deported.
Both later described being held incommunicado and subjected to abuse. Amnesty International reported allegations of torture and ill-treatment, including sexual violence, while United Nations human rights experts issued a communication to the Tanzanian government detailing allegations of enforced disappearance, torture and other abuses. These were allegations documented by the organisations and UN experts, not judicial findings.
The aftermath of the 2025 elections
Tanzania’s political crisis intensified following the October 29, 2025 general election, which was marked by restrictions on opposition participation and deadly post-election violence.
The African Union Election Observation Mission concluded that the elections did not comply with AU democratic principles and international standards. It cited restrictions on political competition, shortcomings in the electoral framework and an internet shutdown that disrupted observation.
The disputed vote triggered protests, arrests and a security crackdown. Human Rights Watch reported that police and people in civilian clothing killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders.
A year later, the organisation said authorities had yet to make arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the election.
A presidential Commission of Inquiry reported that 518 people died from unnatural causes during the unrest. Its chairman, retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman, said the figure might not be conclusive.
The commission also recorded allegations that security officers shot people in their homes and shops. Human Rights Watch criticised the inquiry for failing to meaningfully scrutinise the conduct of security forces.
The figures remain contested. Chadema and other sources have reported higher death tolls, although these estimates have not been independently established.
A CNN investigation published on November 20, 2025, analysed geolocated videos, audio evidence and witness accounts showing police and armed men shooting at protesters, including some who appeared unarmed.
It also documented evidence supporting witness accounts of overflowing morgues and possible mass graves. The Tanzanian government disputed aspects of the reporting.
Kenya’s responsibility
Mwaipaya’s disappearance raises questions about Kenya’s responsibility to protect foreign nationals within its territory, particularly those fleeing political persecution.
Kenya has long provided refuge to activists and opposition figures escaping repression elsewhere in the region. However, the cases of Mwaipaya and Sarungi have raised concerns about whether that protection can be guaranteed when critics of neighbouring governments are allegedly targeted on Kenyan soil.
The Kenyan authorities must establish Mwaipaya’s whereabouts, investigate the circumstances of his disappearance and identify those responsible. Tanzania, meanwhile, must address allegations that its critics are being pursued beyond its borders.
For Tanzanian human rights lawyer Tito Magoti, the disappearances are part of a wider human rights crisis facing the country.
“Tanzanians are not free. Abduction is one side of the coin. There are plenty of other atrocities committed against Tanzanians and they run hand in hand with the abductions. It starts there. You abduct, you torture, you extrajudicially kill, persecute through judicial forums, sexual assault and more, so the state of political freedom is in limbo,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Taiwan votes in local elections to choose mayors, other leaders
noticias.resumen: Key mayoral race in Taipei, a stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang, tests the governing Democratic Progressive Party.
noticias.texto:
Taiwan votes in local elections to choose mayors, other leaders
Key mayoral race in Taipei, a stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang, tests the governing Democratic Progressive Party.
Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election that has been unusually competitive in some of the island’s biggest cities.
Polls opened at 8am (00:00 GMT) on Saturday and will close at 4pm (08:00 GMT), with results expected early in the evening.
Voters are casting ballots at schools, temples and community centres.
About 11,000 positions are at stake in the “nine-in-one” elections, named for the nine categories of local government posts being contested.
Taipei mayoral race
A key contest is for the mayor of the capital, Taipei, a traditional stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).
Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT, who won by a double-digit margin in the last election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate, faces a strong challenge from Puma Shen of the governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
Shen is an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare. China has denounced him, and Chinese police say he is wanted for “separatism”. He entered the race as the underdog, but has drawn huge crowds at his rallies.
Shen’s victory in the KMT’s heartland could be seen as “quite shameful” in Beijing, said Austin Wang, a political scientist at the University of Nevada.
Chiang told supporters the race was “very close”.
Shen cancelled a final rally over traffic concerns and held an online event instead, which drew more than 500,000 viewers on YouTube. President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP also urged voters at a rally in neighbouring New Taipei City to back the party’s candidates there.
Other notable races are in New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous city, and Kaohsiung, in the south. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.
China’s pressure
The vote will not directly change Taiwan’s China policy, and campaigns have focused on local issues such as transport, childcare and the environment.
Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its own territory, has repeatedly weighed in, and the vote is being closely watched there.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense counted some 33 sorties from China’s People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has warned that Beijing is trying to influence the outcome through “cognitive warfare” and “transnational repression”.
China’s Defence Ministry said this week that “reunification” is an unstoppable trend.
In the last local elections four years ago, the KMT won 14 cities and counties, the DPP five and other parties or independents three. The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims.
Analysts say local results are an unreliable guide to the outcome of the next presidential election, due in early 2028. Lai is expected to seek a second term.
The KMT could begin debating its presidential ticket soon after the vote. The likely candidates include outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.
KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April, is also seen as a possible challenger, though she could face pressure to step down if the party does badly.

noticias.titulo: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
noticias.resumen: Anger and frustration erupt over record-high electricity rates, surging cost of living and deteriorating basic services.
noticias.texto:
Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
Anger and frustration erupt over record-high electricity rates, surging cost of living and deteriorating basic services.
Thousands of Puerto Ricans have protested in the capital, San Juan, as anger and frustration erupted over record-high electricity rates, the surging cost of living, deteriorating basic services and other issues.
Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined Friday’s protest organised by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organisations. The crowds gathered in front of a mall for what organisers dubbed the “Day of National Outrage”.
Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.
Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radames Garcia Badillo said: “Where to start? The outrage is absolute.”
He said that power and water services are unreliable and that his neighbourhood goes dark at least once a week for several hours. He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living.
“We’re buying less because things are extremely expensive,” he said. “For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch.”
The protest, one of the largest in the US territory since Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez took office in January 2025, grew throughout the day as demonstrators took over one of the island’s main highways, forcing its closure.
Organisers estimated that some 8,000 people took part, according to local media.
Many in the crowd waved or wore the Puerto Rican flag. Some chose the flag from before the island became a US commonwealth in 1952, often a sign of cultural pride and sometimes of resistance.
Soaring electricity bills
“Things have never been good in Puerto Rico, but they keep getting worse,” said Veronica Ishtar, a visual arts student.
This week alone, she said the power in her neighbourhood went out 12 times.
In addition, monthly electricity bills for some residential customers recently rose about 18 percent, with the new rate per kilowatt-hour far surpassing the average for residential customers on the US mainland, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Some protesters blamed Luma Energy, a private company that oversees the transmission and distribution of power on the island.
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court approved a move to cancel the government’s contract with Luma on Wednesday, but many now worry about what comes next.
Puerto Rico’s Association of Industries said the cancellation could discourage private investment and jeopardise existing projects as crews continue to repair a grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.
The leaders of several groups that organised the protest pledged to keep pushing for change.
“We must begin to channel the rage,” said Hernaliz Vazquez, executive director of Sierra Club Puerto Rico. “We must begin to organise the indignation felt by people who do not know what to do.”

noticias.titulo: At least eight found dead on migrant boat off Spain’s Canary Islands
noticias.resumen: Six people airlifted to hospital in serious condition, Spanish rescue service says.
noticias.texto:
At least eight found dead on migrant boat off Spain’s Canary Islands
Six people airlifted to hospital in serious condition, Spanish rescue service says.
At least eight migrants have been found dead on a boat carrying about 100 people that was rescued near Spain’s Canary Islands, the Spanish maritime rescue service has said.
The rescue service said on Friday that between eight and 10 bodies were found on board and that six people were airlifted to hospital in serious condition.
The boat was found 39 nautical miles (72km) south of the island of El Hierro and was being towed to the port of La Estaca.
Separately, 84 survivors from another boat came ashore at La Restinga, El Hierro’s main port, which has a reception centre and field hospital for migrants.
The Canary Islands are a Spanish region in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of northwest Africa. Anyone who lands there reaches Spanish and European Union territory, which has made the islands a main entry point for migrants from West Africa.
Arrivals hit a record of more than 46,000 in 2024 before falling after tighter surveillance and cooperation with countries of origin and transit.
Patrols off Senegal, Mauritania and Morocco have pushed departures further south to The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau and Guinea, making the crossing longer and more dangerous.
Record arrivals
Arrivals in the Canary Islands have accelerated since October, with a record 2,100 people reaching the islands in a single day earlier this week, mostly on El Hierro, which has 11,400 residents.
Authorities there declared an emergency earlier this month, and rescuers brought in nearly 1,500 people in a single day on November 14.
“The humanitarian emergency doesn’t start on El Hierro, but on the shores of Senegal and Gambia, where we have to act,” regional leader Fernando Clavijo said on X.
He expressed “a lot of pain and feeling of impotence” over the deaths and demanded action from the Spanish government and the European Commission.
A campaign issue
The deaths come two days before Spain’s general elections on Sunday, in which immigration has become a defining issue.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is one of Europe’s most vocal advocates of the economic benefits of immigration, while the right, which leads in the polls, wants far tighter controls.
Thousands of migrants try the Atlantic crossing each year from West Africa in overcrowded boats, despite rough seas and strong currents.
It is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes, and arrivals usually rise between September and November, when sea conditions are more favourable.

noticias.titulo: Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI?
noticias.resumen: Voters will decide on Saturday whether to scrap the country's 'nuclear-free homeland' policy.
noticias.texto:
Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI?
Voters will decide whether to scrap the country’s ‘nuclear-free homeland’ policy on Saturday.
Voters in Taiwan are set to decide whether to bring back nuclear power – 18 months after its last operational reactor was shut down.
A referendum on the issue is being held alongside local elections on Saturday. It is the island’s fourth vote on nuclear power in just eight years.
It comes as demand for electricity to fuel the country’s burgeoning computer chip industry soars and concern grows about how Taiwan would keep its lights on if China, which claims the island as its own territory, cut it off amid escalating tensions.
Here is what we know.
What is the referendum about?
Voters are being asked whether the government should return to using nuclear power to boost the economy. That would mean abolishing the country’s longstanding “nuclear-free homeland” policy.
The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) proposed the referendum and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is also backing it. The legislature approved the referendum in August and the Central Election Commission signed it off on August 28.
To pass, ‘yes’ votes must outnumber ‘no’ votes and exceed a quarter of all eligible voters.
The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), which has long had a policy of no nuclear power in its mandate, is urging ‘no’. DPP legislator Chen Pei-yu called the referendum unnecessary, saying lawmakers could change the policy by amending existing laws instead.
Why did Taiwan give up nuclear power?
Taiwan once relied heavily on nuclear power. In 1985, its three plants produced 52 percent of the nation’s electricity.
Nuclear power then became one of the most partisan issues in Taiwanese politics. Lev Nachman, an assistant professor at the Graduate Institute of National Development at National Taiwan University, said the divide goes back to the DPP’s founding.
“There was a major group of environmentalists that were part of the party that were very anti-nuclear,” Nachman told Al Jazeera. The nuclear industry, by contrast, was built and run under the KMT.
Polarisation turned that into “a very green-versus-blue issue”, Nachman said, referring to the colours of the DPP and the KMT.
Safety fears run deep. Nachman said Taiwan watched the 2011 Fukushima nuclear plant meltdown in neighbouring Japan very closely.
“There is this sort of fear of any sort of nuclear reaction that would ever happen in Taiwan would just devastate the entire island,” he said. Active geological fault lines run across Taiwan and the question of how to dispose of nuclear waste remains unresolved.
The DPP has governed since 2016, partly on a pledge to phase out nuclear power. In May last year, Taiwan shut down its last reactor at Maanshan in Pingtung County.
Why is nuclear power back on the agenda?
Public opinion has been mixed in three previous referendums. In 2018, voters opted to scrap a legal deadline for phasing out nuclear power. But in 2021, they rejected restarting construction on an unfinished fourth nuclear plant. In August last year, a majority vote to restart the Maanshan plant was voided due to low turnout.
Now, nuclear power is back on the agenda because surging electricity demand from Taiwan’s semiconductor and AI industries, along with growing fears about energy security and over-reliance on imported fuel, have renewed the debate over how the island keeps the lights on in an emergency.
According to the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Taiwan imports more than 97 percent of its energy. Natural gas generates about 43 percent of its electricity and coal about 35 percent. Both arrive by ship.
Taiwan only has about 11 days of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in reserve. Japan and South Korea hold between 14 and 20 days.
“There’s two sides to it,” Nachman said. The first is energy security: “If China actually blockades Taiwan and cuts off access to the outside world, then Taiwan only has so much energy it can rely on.”
The second is the chip industry, which requires huge amounts of power and “that’s only going to increase over time”, he said.
The war with Iran this year has added to the pressure by disrupting LNG shipments from the Middle East.
Will the ruling party change its stance?
The DPP has already started to shift. In March, President William Lai Ching-te said the government would begin the process of restarting the Maanshan and Kuosheng plants. He cited AI-driven demand and conflicts abroad causing disruption to energy supplies.
On September 24, the Nuclear Safety Commission approved state-owned Taipower’s restart plan for Maanshan. Further safety assessments are still needed before it can operate again.
Nachman said Lai has tried to push his party to rethink its “very dogmatic anti-nuclear stance”. The question is whether DPP voters have come around.
Nuclear power is not Taiwan’s first choice for filling the gap, however. “Investment in LNG – that’s still Taiwan’s kind of number one goal,” Nachman said.
How important is Taiwan’s microchip industry?
Taiwan is the most important link in the global AI supply chain.
It makes more than 90 percent of the world’s most advanced semiconductors, nearly all of them at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). TSMC has more than 60 percent of the global contract chipmaking market.
Its customers include Nvidia – the world’s most valuable semiconductor company – AMD and Apple. TSMC makes Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin AI processors, and Taiwanese firms such as Foxconn and Quanta build most of the world’s AI servers.
That uses huge amounts of electricity and water. In September, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry used more than 4.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity for the first time. That was up 11.55 percent from a year earlier, driven by AI demand.
S&P Global estimated that TSMC alone used about 8 percent of Taiwan’s electricity in 2023. That share could rise to almost 24 percent by 2030, it added.
Nachman cautioned against seeing the referendum only through the demand for microchips and semiconductors. “In today’s media, Taiwan has become a single issue, just about semiconductors,” he said. “For a lot of people in Taiwan, the semiconductors aren’t even the priority. It really is the security side.”
Will China object to Taiwan having nuclear power?
Probably not. Beijing does not appear to have commented on the referendum itself.
“The nuclear issue is a completely separate issue from anything related to China,” Nachman said. “It’s much more a matter of domestic politics.”
China has, however, used Taiwan’s energy weakness in its messaging. In March, Chen Binhua, a spokesman for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said closer integration with China could help solve Taiwan’s energy problems. He pointed to the island’s reliance on oil and gas from the Middle East.
Taipei rejects unification with Beijing. Analysts writing in The Diplomat called the offer an exercise in optics.
However, it remains a top priority for China. During a speech in Beijing on November 12, President Xi Jinping once again stated that Taiwan and China must be reunified.
The referendum is about civilian power reactors, not weapons. Asked whether Taiwan might seek a nuclear weapon, Nachman said: “No, of course not. This is just about nuclear power.”
Taiwan did secretly pursue nuclear weapons in the 1970s and 1980s. The programme was shut down in 1988 under US pressure, after a senior nuclear scientist, Chang Hsien-yi, defected to the United States.
Since then, Taiwan’s leaders have consistently stated that they will not seek nuclear weapons. Its nuclear facilities are inspected under an arrangement between Taiwan, the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
The bigger worry is a blockade by China if it seeks to press reunification in the future. Nachman said large military drills and naval patrols China has held around Taiwan since US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit in 2022 have all rehearsed one.
Will the referendum pass and what happens next?
Nachman said he is sceptical. “We keep doing it over and over again and it still doesn’t usually pass,” he said. “So my expectations are actually fairly low.”
The outcome will depend on DPP supporters. “It’s really more a matter of whether or not green voters have come around to it,” Nachman said.
If the referendum does pass, he said Lai and the DPP “would probably be largely okay with it”.
The restart process is already under way either way. Supporters say reactors could be running again within 18 months to three years. Opponents say a restart could take five to 10 years and cost several hundred billion New Taiwan dollars.
Results are expected on Saturday night.

noticias.titulo: Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more than 123 starvation deaths
noticias.resumen: Paul Mackenzie, already serving 200 years, is the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
noticias.texto:
Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more than 123 starvation deaths
Paul Mackenzie, already serving 200 years, is the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.
Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.
Earlier convictions
On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.
He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.
The Shakahola deaths
Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.
He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death to meet Jesus before the end of the world.
Police arrested him in 2023 after a tip-off, and authorities began uncovering more than 400 bodies. People familiar with the cult told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the starvation in three phases: children first, then women and young men, and finally, the remaining men.
Mackenzie had been arrested twice before, in connection with the deaths of children, and released.
Calls for oversight
The killings have shocked Kenya and led to calls for tighter oversight of religious groups.
President William Ruto said in 2023 that he took responsibility as head of state for the government’s failure to prevent the deaths.
Other mass killings linked to cults include one in Uganda in 2000, when a doomsday group killed more than 700 people, and the 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader ordered more than 900 followers to drink poison, Reuters said.

noticias.titulo: US military says it disabled merchant ship trying to breach Iran blockade
noticias.resumen: The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed.
noticias.texto:
US military says it disabled merchant ship trying to breach Iran blockade
The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed.
The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.
Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.
US officials say the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel’s destination as Singapore. It is at least the 15th vessel the US military has publicly acknowledged disabling since the blockade began in April, and the sixth since it resumed it in July. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.
The claims could not be independently verified.
The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said on Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations “that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region’s waters”.
American blockade action
The US military has maintained a sizeable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.
American ships have been blockading Iranian ports since April, although the blockade was temporarily lifted during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the US military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabled those that refuse to comply.
CENTCOM, which has its headquarters in Florida, has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.

‘Activists of rhythm’: Fighting Spain’s far-right through art
NewsFeed
‘Activists of rhythm’: Fighting Spain’s far-right through art
