noticias.titulo: Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
noticias.resumen: Flour and oil still reach markets in Hodeidah and Sanaa. But high costs and lack of work and aid put it out of reach.
noticias.texto:
Why are families going hungry in northern Yemen even where food is on sale?
Flour and oil still reach markets in Hodeidah and Sanaa. But rising costs, scarce work and loss of food aid put them out of reach.
Umm Sami, a widow raising four children in Yemen’s Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, sells household goods and takes on occasional domestic work to feed her family. Rising prices have changed how she shops. “Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera.
Food is still on the shelves. It was available in the markets that monitors could reach in September, but families had less money to spend, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report, a humanitarian and food security assessment. Across Houthi-controlled areas like Hodeidah, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent, or $91, more that month than in August, its highest level in a year.
Families on both sides of the front lines are struggling, and prices are rising faster in the government-held south, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET). What sets the Houthi-controlled north apart is how little families there can earn and how little help is left.
Most households in and around northern towns find only five to 10 days of paid work a month, FEWS NET reported in October. The UN World Food Programme’s (WFP) food assistance in Houthi-held areas has been suspended since September 2025, FEWS NET said. By mid-September 2026, WFP had begun a distribution round in government-held areas that aimed to reach about 1.7 million people.
In the last nationwide hunger analysis by UN agencies and their partners, published in mid-2025, the only people projected to face catastrophic hunger, about 41,000, were in four districts of Amran, Hodeidah and Hajjah governorates – all under Houthi control.
On Friday, the WFP and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) named Yemen among its hunger hotspots of highest concern for the six months ending May 2027.
As fighting spreads and aid dries up, we look at why food on sale in northern Yemen is slipping out of reach of the families who need it.
Why are some families in Hodeidah buying food one day at a time?
Because a day’s work – when there is any – no longer pays for a day’s food.
Ahmed Arjash drives a rented motorcycle taxi near Hodeidah’s Othman market to support his family of six. Many of his former customers now walk to save the fare. “Now, my daily earnings barely cover the fuel or the rent for the motorcycle,” he told Al Jazeera.
Saleh, a construction worker paid by the day, said some days pass without anyone hiring him. “If I work one day, the wage is not enough to cover the family’s needs for several days with prices this high,” he said.
Fishing pays less, too. Salem, a fisherman in his 30s, said fuel, boats and equipment cost him more while fewer customers could afford his catch. “Many families no longer buy fish as they used to,” he said. On some trips, he barely earns back what it costs to go to sea.
Families are adjusting by eating less. In Hodeidah’s poorest neighbourhoods, many skip meals or go without meat, fish, milk and fruit, Al Jazeera found.
In Houthi-held areas, FEWS NET reported that higher taxes on street vendors and shops had already reduced demand for labour in September. In its outlook through May 2027, it expected more small businesses to close and those that stayed open to hire fewer workers.
How does food reach shops in northern Yemen, and what makes the journey more expensive?
Almost all of it comes by sea, and each step from ship to shop now costs more. Yemen imports about 90 percent of its food, according to WFP. Hodeidah is the main port supplying the Houthi-held north, including Sanaa.
Food has kept arriving – data shows imports into Houthi-held areas rose 10 percent between June and August compared with the previous three months and doubled year-on-year – but fuel has not.
Fuel imports fell about 85 percent year-on-year in August, with no recorded arrivals of diesel or petrol through northern ports, according to the FAO. In September, the Houthi authorities raised the price of petrol by about 10 percent, the first increase in four years, Al Jazeera reported. Bread prices in Houthi-held areas rose 25 percent that month, FEWS NET said.
The ports themselves have come under attack. On November 2, the Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said Saudi aircraft had hit a pier and a commercial ship at Ras Isa port, north of Hodeidah, the news agency AFP reported. On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had attacked “operational capabilities” in Hodeidah, and the Houthis threatened to retaliate against Saudi Red Sea ports. Hodeidah port remains open, Al Jazeera reported. How the latest attacks will affect deliveries remains unclear.
Moving goods inland has also become slower and costlier. A truck travelling between the south and the north “now takes up to a week to reach its final destination”, Saleh Abdullah, a shopkeeper in Sanaa, told Al Jazeera in September. Before the renewed fighting, the trip took three days or less. Customers pay the extra transport and fuel costs, he said. “Whether it is the flour, the baby milk, the fruits, the vegetables, or anything else.”
When families cannot afford food, what stops aid from reaching them?
In the north, the main source of food aid has been switched off. WFP suspended its activities in Houthi-controlled areas in September 2025 after the group detained UN staff. Last month, WFP said 73 UN personnel, 38 of them its own staff, remained in detention.
Other aid organisations still operate in the north, but funding cuts and restrictions limit their reach.
On Thursday, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said a handful of overstretched and underfunded Yemeni and international organisations were the only remaining lifeline for millions there.
Funding cuts, sanctions and the UN’s pause in operations had all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, it added. The NRC said donors had provided just 16 percent of the money sought for food security across Yemen this year.
What does the UN’s new hunger warning tell us about northern Yemen?
The latest FAO–WFP report warns that fighting and economic hardship threaten to deepen hunger through May 2027. It names economic hardship among the threats, but it cannot say how many people in the north are going hungry. FAO and WFP said conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather drove the risk in the five hotspots of highest concern, the Reuters news agency reported.
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), the UN-backed system for measuring hunger, has not published a recent analysis of Houthi-held areas. Its latest figures – 5.4 million people facing crisis levels of hunger or worse between October and December, including 1.8 million at the more severe emergency level – cover government-held areas only.
In June 2025, the IPC projected that 18.1 million people in Yemen would face crisis levels of hunger or worse between September 2025 and February 2026. That was 52 percent of the population covered by the nationwide analysis.
FEWS NET expects emergency levels of hunger to persist in Hodeidah and Hajjah through May 2027.
At that level, families face large gaps in what they eat, or must sell what they need to make a living to buy food. The network’s gravest warning concerns Taiz, a government-held city besieged by Houthi forces, where it sees a credible risk of famine between February and May if the siege is prolonged and tightened.
In Hodeidah, the market still has flour. For families like Umm Sami’s, the question is how little of it they can afford. “Even bread has become a burden,” she said.

noticias.titulo: Polls open in Taiwan's closely watched local elections
noticias.resumen: Polls have opened for local elections in Taiwan. While campaigners have stayed away from the topic of China and focused on issues like transport and childcare, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.
noticias.texto:
Polls open in Taiwan's closely watched local elections
November 28, 2026
Taiwan's voters begun choosing mayors and county chiefs in local elections on Saturday that may gauge the mood ahead of the island's 2028 presidential elections.
Polls close at 4 p.m. (0800 UTC/GMT) and results are expected by early evening. Winners will serve four-year terms.
Most candidates are from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) or the Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT. The latter has traditionally performed better in local elections and favors closer ties with China.
President Lai Ching-te has campaigned for candidates from his DPP.
Closely watched in Beijing
China is paying close attention, despite not currently featuring as a key campaign issue. Taiwan's government warned its people to be vigilant against fake news on social media, citing a Chinese disinformation campaign.
Taiwan's 22 cities and counties are currently focused on issues such as transport, childcare and the environment. While these issues do not directly impact the China policy, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.
China denounced the governing Democratic Progressive candidate for Taipei's mayoral race, Puma Shen, who is wanted by Chinese police for alleged "separatist activities." He entered the mayoral race as an underdog but has managed to ride a political wave that drew huge crowds to his campaign rallies.
Earlier this month, Shen said Chinese police had never contacted him and that whoever wins, Taipei's election would be a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from Beijing.
If Shen wins, he would be the capital city's first DPP mayor in nearly 30 years. This result could be seen as "quite shameful" in Beijing, according to Austin Wang, political science professor at the University of Nevada.
China claims Taiwan as part of its territory under its "One China" principle and has recently increased pressure on Taiwan to accept its sovereignty claims, threatening force to seize the island.
Taipei's incumbent and KMT member, Mayor Chiang Wan-an has campaigned against Shen, also pulling in thousands of supporters to his rallies. In the last election, KMT thrashed DPP, winning 14 of the 22 cities and counties while the DPP won only five. Chiang is also seen as a potential future presidential candidate.
What impact could the vote have on presidential elections?
Analysts have cautioned that the local elections are not a reliable barometer of how people might vote for the presidential elections in 2028. Still, Saturday's results could influence the selection process for the KMT presidential candidate.
The DPP is likely to rally behind President Lai for a reelection.
The most likely KMT candidates are Taichung's outgoing Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.
KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who's pro-Beijing stance has even alienated her from many in the party, is also viewed as a potential challenger for the party's nomination. However, she could face pressure to step down if KMT performs poorly in the local elections.

noticias.titulo: Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
noticias.resumen: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told people to turn out in large numbers so the country does not go "backwards." Polls suggest an end to his eight-year leftist leadership of Spain.
noticias.texto:
Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election
November 28, 2026
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday hit the campaign trail one last time before Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday, telling people to "vote, vote, vote" to make sure the country doesn't go "backwards."
Opinion polls point to a change in government, with the conservative People's Party (PP) slated to come out on top, bringing an end to Sanchez's eight years of leftist leadership.
Spain's general election this Sunday is also crucial because it kicks off a round of elections on the continentand because it is yet another test of the region's shift to the right.
The PP would potentially have to rely on support from the far-right anti-immigration Vox party to form the next government in Spain.
There's also a chance that the election ends in a hung parliament, with neither the right-wing coalition nor the left bloc securing a majority.
Sanchez has so far campaigned on a platform of having boosted the Spanish economy when its European Union partners were struggling.
He has pointed to his policies of having increased the minimum wage and having lifted pensions in line with inflation.
But people are frustrated that the cost of living has soared and that they're not able to enjoy the fruits of economic growth, with many unable to leave their parents' house because of very high rental prices.
Sanchez doubles down on attempt to appeal to leftist voters
Sanchez said during his final rally in Madrid that the "elections are about moving Spain forward, not moving it backwards."
He doubled down on an attempt to appeal to left-leaning voters, telling them that a right coalition government, with far-right members in parliament, would reverse the years of social progress and gut public services.
Oscar-winning Spanish film director Pedro Almodovar was also at the rally this evening.
Sanchez wore a red T-shirt that said "the power of the people," telling people that a "progressive majority is within our reach."
Sanchez has also become the standard-bearer for Europeans frustrated with the Trump administration.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo dismisses Sanchez's campaign of 'fear'
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has said that he wants to maintain good relations with US President Donald Trump, dismissed Sanchez's campaign of "fear."
Feijoo won the most seats during elections in 2023, but he was not able to form a government.
"And when a government has nothing to offer but fear, it means it has nothing else left to offer," he told supporters at his campaign finale in the southern city of Seville.
"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," said Feijoo, who built his career running central public bodies and the northwestern Galicia region.
He has advocated for tough immigration policies and stronger border management.
Santiago Abascal, the leader of the Vox party, favors a much tougher approach, with his party having advocated for mass deportations.
Addressing a closing rally at a bullring in the eastern city of Valencia, Abascal told supporters not to "vote out of fear. Vote with courage."
"What we are up against is a criminal mafia led by a ruthless boss, a liar," he said, referring to the corruption scandals that have surrounded Sanchez and his government.

noticias.titulo: US disables ship in Gulf of Oman under Iran blockade
noticias.resumen: The United States said it was continuing "to strictly enforce the blockade" of Iran's ports. Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over a strike that killed two Italian technicians.
noticias.texto:
US disables ship in Gulf of Oman under Iran blockade
November 28, 2026
The United States military on Friday announced it had fired at a ship in the Gulf of Oman that it said was violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports.
A US aircraft fired "precision munitions" in the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer, US Central Command (CENTCOM), said, adding that it "continues to strictly enforce the [US] blockade."
CENTCOM oversees US forces in the Middle East.
The statement said that "the ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled" and stressed that "the civilian crew was unharmed."
It said that the ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas.
The US blockade has disabled six ships and redirected 158 others.
Washington launched its blockade of Iranian ports in mid-July following the collapse of an agreement with Tehran.
The war broke out in February after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, which prompted Tehran to impose its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
Kuwait summons Iran ambassador over strike on military site
Meanwhile, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador after a Thursday drone strike killed two Italian technicians at a Kuwaiti military site.
A Kuwaiti citizen and a Pakistani citizen were also injured and hospitalized in the attack.
Iran has denied responsibility for the strike.
Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said Deputy Foreign Minister Hamad Al-Mashaan condemned the "continued Iranian attacks" and said Kuwait reserved its right to self-defense.
The two technicians worked for Rheinmetall Italia, a subsidiary of the German defense firm Rheinmetall.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, calling on "all parties to exercise restraint."
Guterres is "deeply concerned by the continued escalation in the region," according to his spokesman, Stephane Dujarric. "Renewed hostilities would have devastating consequences for the region and beyond."

noticias.titulo: Russia-Ukraine war extends to Baltic, Mediterranean
noticias.resumen: By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Ukraine is trying to increase the pressure on Russia and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?
noticias.texto:
Russia-Ukraine war extends to Baltic, Mediterranean
November 26, 2026
First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.
Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?
It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.
And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.
Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.
Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.
Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region
Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.
Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."
Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.
Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.
The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.
Could war become omnipresent?
"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.
"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."
Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.
In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.
Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."
Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."
She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.
She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Uganda begins Africa's first mRNA Ebola vaccine trial
noticias.resumen: An experimental mRNA vaccine developed by Moderna is being tested on 224 volunteers in Uganda as health authorities seek to combat a deadly Ebola outbreak that has claimed thousands of lives in neighbouring DRC.
noticias.texto:
An experimental mRNA vaccine developed by Moderna is being tested on 224 volunteers in Uganda as health authorities seek to combat a deadly Ebola outbreak that has claimed thousands of lives in neighbouring DRC.
Uganda has begun clinical trials of an experimental vaccine targeting the Ebola strain responsible for the ongoing outbreak in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the country's virus research institute announced on Friday.
The outbreak, caused by the less common Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has killed more than 5,700 people, with over 11,000 cases recorded since May, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). No vaccines or treatments are currently approved for this strain.
Trials of two experimental vaccines are scheduled to begin on Monday in eastern DRC, the epicentre of the outbreak, targeting people who have been in contact with infected individuals and those considered at high risk of infection.
Uganda has already begun testing one of the two vaccines, developed by US pharmaceutical company Moderna using the mRNA technology widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Uganda Virus Research Institute said in a statement it had "launched Africa's first mRNA Phase I clinical trial... in collaboration with Moderna of an investigational vaccine against Bundibugyo ebolavirus".
The study will involve 224 healthy volunteers aged between one and 65 to assess the vaccine's safety and its ability to trigger an immune response.
Uganda, which shares a long and porous border with eastern DRC, managed to contain the spread of the virus after recording imported cases earlier this year.
The country was declared Ebola-free in August after recording 20 infections and two deaths.
Gavi secures 1.5 million doses of experimental Ebola vaccine
Meanwhile, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has signed a purchase commitment with India's Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses of the other experimental vaccine, developed in collaboration with the University of Oxford.
The alliance aims to have "hundreds of thousands" of doses ready for distribution if clinical trials prove successful and the vaccine is approved by the WHO and DRC government.
"We're investing in it, hoping that the signals will be positive, and if that is the case, we'll have gained months and months on the deployment," Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi's director of global health security, told AFP.
Capobianco said he hoped for trials to conclude "within the first half of 2027" and even "within the first quarter" in a more optimistic scenario.
Gavi also holds a stockpile of 500,000 doses of Ervebo, an existing vaccine against the Zaire strain of Ebola, which is being tested to determine whether it is also effective against Bundibugyo.

noticias.titulo: 9 things you need to read ahead of the Spanish election
noticias.resumen: From understanding the key players to watching Sunday’s results like a pro, here’s everything you need to know.
noticias.texto: Spain is heading into the weekend with bated breath, as Sunday’s snap election could see the country swing to the right after eight years of Socialist rule. Ipsos’ director of research in Spain, Paco Camas, told POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook that turnout could reach a record 75%. And for good reason: There’s a lot at stake. While polls predict the center-right People’s Party will claim victory and — with help from the far-right Vox — topple one of the EU’s last remaining socialist leaders, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez still harbors hopes of holding them off. If a PP-Vox coalition comes to fruition, it’ll mark the first time the far right has governed in Spain since the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975. From understanding the key political players and parties, to watching Sunday’s results like a pro, here’s everything you need to know. (Click on the headlines to read the full reports.) Picture taken in 1936 of Spanish soldiers loyal to the young Republic acclaimed by the crowd as they arrive in Madrid from Vilcavaro to fight against the nationalist troops of General Franco. | AFP via Getty Images 1. Back to 1936? Civil war ghosts haunt Spanish election campaign Ninety years after the outbreak of the civil war, Spain’s campaign for the Nov. 29 election has unmistakable echoes of 1936. Politicians are resurrecting the rhetoric of a conflict that still runs deep in the polarized national psyche, with Sánchez leading crowds in chants of “¡No pasarán!” (“They shall not pass!”), the slogan immortalized by the left-wing forces that resisted Franco’s three-year siege of Madrid. Both far-right leader Santiago Abascal of Vox and Madrid’s regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso of the PP have, in turn, referred to their left-wing opponents as the “Popular Front,” used by the coalition of communist, socialist and republican forces that governed Spain on the eve of the outbreak of the civil war. 2. Surging left-wing Basque separatists brace for showdown with Spain’s right The election is also set to reshape politics in the northern industrial region of the Basque Country, where the bitterly divisive question of independence is boiling up again. Despite a likely right-wing coalition on the cards at the national level, polls in the Basque region project a strong electoral performance by the left-wing separatist EH Bildu coalition. “The majority of the Basque Country is socially progressive and sovereigntist,” Gorka Elejabarrieta, a Bildu lawmaker running for the Spanish parliament in Gipuzkoa, told POLITICO. “Our coalition and movement bring together those two ideas, which are hegemonic in Basque society.” Carles Puigdemont gestures after a press conference in Waterloo, Belgium on Oct. 6, 2026 | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images 3. Return of Spanish right risks reigniting Catalan separatist flame The vote also risks pushing the explosive issue of Catalan independence right back up the political agenda — especially as it comes just days after former regional president Carles Puigdemont announced his plans to return home after nearly a decade of exile in Belgium. After Puigdemont’s separatist drive in Catalonia plunged Spain into a constitutional crisis in 2017-2018, the topic now lies dormant, barely making headlines. But that could change quickly if a conservative coalition comes to power on Nov. 29. “We know that they are certain to cut back our self-governing powers and intervene in Catalan society in a very heavy way,” said Francesc-Marc Álvaro, a candidate for the Senate for the Catalan Republican Left. “This would amount to throwing gasoline on Catalan society.” 4. Far-right Vox sees election as its big chance to reshape Spain Polling third in the race at around 18%, the nationalist, euroskeptic Vox is hailing Sunday’s election as “Spain’s last chance to be Spain again,” and is seeking to remold the country by pushing its people into top ministerial jobs. Vox is on track to make the biggest gains of any major party: While it secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress in 2023, it is now set to double that. Party leader Abascal has insisted the election is a chance to hold on to “the peace, prosperity and freedom that a mafioso government wants to snatch from us forever.” 5. From Madrid to MAGA: How Spain’s Vox forged a right-wing network with global reach Unlike Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz in Hungary or Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, which have spent decades shaping national and European politics, Vox is a relative newcomer, having only entered Spain’s parliament in 2019 . But it is a force on the march. It’s hoping to play an increasingly central role as a bridge linking Europe’s far right to political allies worldwide — from Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast to MAGA in Washington. Though distinct, the groups are bound by a common rejection of the political establishment. “This isn’t about occupying more space. This is a movement,” EU lawmaker and director of the Disenso Foundation Jorge Martín Frías told POLITICO. Illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO 6. Spain’s (likely) next prime minister is the polar opposite of Pedro Sánchez PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo is always keen to play up that he’s the country boy from the lush Atlantic coastal region of Galicia. “Help me finish this journey and I will not fail you … I am still the same: with more gray hairs, more experience, more scars, but with the same commitment,” he told a home crowd earlier this month in the pilgrimage city of Santiago de Compostela. Feijóo’s pitch is that he is the unflashy, sober manager who steadily learned his homespun skills on his northwestern turf as Galicia’s president from 2009 to 2022 — a world apart from the polished showmanship of Sánchez. While Sánchez speaks impeccable English, Feijóo barely speaks a word. While Sánchez became prime minister at 46, Feijóo is 65 and would be the oldest man to win the premiership since Spain’s return to democracy in the 1970s. 7. Feijóo wants to run Spain like a CEO. Not easy with far-right Vox on the board. The PP’s core message that it’s banking on to propel it to victory is being sober, sensible — even slightly dull — managers. Reinforcing the idea that the PP wants to run the EU’s fourth-biggest economy like a competent, unflashy corporation, one senior party official told POLITICO it was “offering a CEO to lead the country.” It’s a simple message with traction after a wave of corruption scandals under Sánchez. But if the next government is a business, Vox will be a maverick on the board. 8. 5 key places that signal where Spain’s election is heading On Sunday, Sánchez risks losing the only province that his Socialist Party has held since the death of Franco, which could be one of multiple historic changes to Spain’s electoral map. From vanishing heartlands to bellwether villages and regional rivalries with national impact, we’ve mapped five key places to watch on election night. An electoral campaign billboard for Spanish Prime Minister and Spanish Socialist Party (PSOE) leader Pedro Sánchez is pictured near the Sagrada Familia Basilica in Barcelona on November 25, 2026. | Manaure Quintero/AFP via Getty Images 9. How to watch the Spanish election like a pro Almost 39 million Spaniards are eligible to vote in the election and turnout is projected to be higher than ever, with many voters seeing the contest as a potential turning point for the country. Feijóo has vowed to bring “the necessary change” to Spain, telling POLITICO that his party and Vox agree that “ sanchismo [Sánchez’s rule] is going to end in our country.” Sánchez, meanwhile, is framing his reelection as a choice between joining a “far-right wave that drives regression” or having Spain “remain a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility.” For real-time updates on the Spanish election, follow POLITICO’s live blog on Sunday night.

noticias.titulo: La Fuerza Aérea de EE.UU. sufrió un hackeo según PBS y NBC
noticias.texto:
La Fuerza Aérea de EE.UU. sufrió un hackeo según PBS y NBC
- El ataque fue contra la plataforma de nube 'Cloud One' de la Fuerza Aérea
- No está claro si alguna información sensible pudo quedar expuesta
La Fuerza Aérea estadounidense sufrió una intrusión cibernética ('hackeo') en una de sus principales plataformas, según reportaron este viernes los canales de televisión PBS y NBC, lo que se suma a una serie de ciberataques a agencias del Gobierno de Estados Unidos.
Los atacantes, no identificados, penetraron una plataforma de información de la nube de la Fuerza Aérea, lo que "podría haber expuesto información militar sensible", reportó NBC al citar a un funcionario del Gobierno de Estados Unidos.
La intrusión ocurrió meses atrás este año y "se mitigó sin interrupciones" al sistema, detalló PBS en su programa 'News Hour', que también reportó que un oficial del Gobierno le confirmó el hecho, aunque sostuvo que no está claro si alguna información quedó expuesta.
El ataque, según este último reporte, fue contra la plataforma de nube 'Cloud One' de la Fuerza Aérea, que pone en orden la defensa aérea, rastrea misiles aéreos y gestiona información del personal.
Ante los informes en la prensa, un portavoz dijo a Fox News que "el Departamento de la Fuerza Aérea no hace comentarios sobre la postura de seguridad, las vulnerabilidades ni el estado operativo de redes y sistemas específicos", además de asegurar que adopta de "manera continua medidas prudentes para proteger la información".
El hecho ocurre tras trascender en la última semana que también ha habido intrusiones cibernéticas contra el FBI, la Agencia Central de Inteligencia (CIA), la Oficina del Director de Inteligencia Nacional de Estados Unidos (ODNI) y el Departamento de Agricultura de Estados Unidos.
Las preocupaciones en el país norteamericano por la infraestructura digital se han elevado este mes en medio de fallas que obligaron a interrumpir el servicio de empresas como Microsoft y el banco JP Morgan, así como un freno de operaciones aéreas por la Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA).
En medio de la crisis, la Casa Blanca relevó al director nacional de ciberseguridad, Sean Cairncross, a quien sustituyó de manera interina la hasta ahora directora de información del Pentágono, Kirsten Davies.

noticias.texto:
La izquierda cierra la campaña ilusionada por la “remontada” con PP y Vox seguros de poder gobernar pese a los patinazos
17
La campaña de las elecciones del 29 de noviembre concluye con una perspectiva de resultados para el domingo que difiere de lo que indicaba la mayoría de las encuestas hace apenas un mes. El PSOE y el Frente Amplio, que aparecían muy lejos de poder reeditar un Gobierno de coalición, tienen ahora la esperanza de culminar una “remontada” que ha cogido vuelo en la última semana, con el colofón del debate a cuatro de este jueves. Una opción que depende también del desempeño del resto de partidos del bloque progresista. En el campo contrario, PP y Vox confían en que las urnas no depararán sorpresas y que Alberto Núñez Feijóo llegará a la Moncloa, esta vez sí, con la duda de si la extrema derecha volverá a un Gobierno que no toca desde el final de la dictadura.
En el PP llegan al final de la campaña electoral como hace tres años: convencidos de que arrasarán en las urnas y gobernarán sin ningún problema, aunque con Vox. Pese a los errores de la campaña, desde el plante a TVE y Silvia Intxaurrondo al “y usted, calladita” de Feijóo a Ada Colau en el debate a cuatro, no hay nadie en el partido que tenga una opinión divergente.
Los principales dirigentes del partido se esfuerzan por aparentar en público que no está todo hecho. El equipo de campaña teme el efecto desmovilizador de la euforia, y se empeña en vender que hay opciones de un empate con la izquierda. Pero la proliferación de actos hace imposible ocultar que están convencidos de gobernar.
Lo hizo el propio candidato, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, el miércoles en un acto en Madrid junto a Isabel Díaz Ayuso. El mitin que prometía ser el más concurrido junto al de la plaza de toros de Valencia dejó ver cientos de asientos vacíos en las gradas. Con un tono impostado, el líder del PP aseguró que no volverá a quedarse a las puertas de la Moncloa, como le pasó en 2023.
“Esta vez sí, queridos amigos”, dijo. “No es que la otra vez no hubiéramos ganado”, añadió. “No es que la otra vez no hubiésemos sacado 16 escaños más que el PSOE y mayoría absoluta en el Senado”, expuso. “No. Lo que pasa es que esta vez no van a poder sumar con nadie. No van a poder gobernar con nadie”, concluyó.
Las encuestas que maneja el PP dan a Feijóo ganador el 29N, con el PSOE muy lejos y con Vox menos fuerte de lo que se preveía. Las derechas, según apuntan las fuentes del PP consultadas, sumarían una mayoría muy holgada. Feijóo, seguro de su triunfo, llegó a prometer este jueves ante 10 millones de espectadores que dimitirá si no consigue gobernar.
Y, aun así, los nervios se han apoderado del partido a lo largo de una campaña desigual y con decisiones polémicas.
Feijóo ha plantado a RTVE tanto en las entrevistas informativas (no ha acudido ni a TVE ni a RNE) como en otros formatos, como ‘La Revuelta’, cuya invitación también declinó. A cambio, el líder del PP se ha dejado ver en programas y medios deportivos (‘Marca’, ‘As’, ‘El chiringuito’, ‘Tiempo de juego’) o en podcast (Jordi Wild, Plex, ‘Línea de cal’).
El PP también ha exprimido las redes sociales. Su equipo ha jugado a convertir en un producto de consumo para jóvenes en TikTok al Feijóo que vende gestión, experiencia, “trazabilidad”, y que presume de ser un “señor del rural” que nunca ha estudiado inglés. Para ello, lo han transfigurado en un remedo de Kobe Bryant, en un ‘anime’ imitando a Lula da Silva o en el rapero ‘Anatop at’.
Feijóo se ha cuidado de hacer muchas propuestas concretas en la campaña, más allá del programa electoral, que recoge más de 400 medidas. Y algunas de las que ha hecho, como la deflactación del IRPF (una rebaja del impuesto de la renta), las ha matizado en el tramo final. Este viernes, el líder del PP optó por una entrevista en la Cope para reemplazar la que no quiso dar a Intxaurrondo (TVE). “La deflactación del impuesto de la renta lo vamos a hacer en función de las capacidades presupuestarias y de ingresos que nos quede”, explicó.
Unas horas antes, el responsable económico de Vox, José María Figaredo, prometía un recorte del gasto público del 50%. Unos 112.000 millones de euros. Feijóo no reclamó en el debate a Santiago Abascal que condenara la violencia machista. Ambos partidos, PP y Vox, se han evitado durante toda la campaña. No han confrontado (con la excepción de Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo) ni se han hecho guiños. Como si el otro no existiera para evitar lo inevitable: que la gente les perciba como un 'pack' indivisible.
Este viernes, Feijóo cerró la campaña en Sevilla, en su primera y única visita al feudo del presidente andaluz Juan Manuel Moreno, y ha hecho una apelación directa al votante de izquierdas. “No les voy a engañar, voy a ser el presidente de todos”, dijo. Y eso que no ha explicado en ningún momento qué tipo de alianza quiere cerrar con Vox si ambos suman mayoría suficiente para investirle.
“No os pido que dejéis de sentiros de izquierdas”, dijo. “Sé que no os gusta lo que veis, porque sé que vosotros no votasteis a esto”, añadió.“Tu voto también dice lo que no estás dispuesto a tolerar. No te quedes en casa y vota una opción honesta. Préstanos tu voto para volver a la honestidad”, concluyó.
El optimismo entre los asistentes a los actos es evidente. Este viernes, en Sevilla, miles de personas le gritaron el habitual “se nota, se siente, Feijóo presidente”. “Qué razón tienen”, replicó el líder del PP desde el atril, convencido de su triunfo el domingo.
Sánchez, optimismo contra las encuestas
En las filas socialistas, el estado de ánimo es inversamente proporcional a la media de las encuestas. El equipo electoral de Pedro Sánchez llega a la víspera del 29N convencido de haber llevado a cabo “la mejor campaña de la historia del PSOE”. Y se basan en datos de audiencia de televisión, de tráfico en redes, de asistencia a mítines y también en sus encuestas internas para trasladar el convencimiento de que el domingo puede volver a producirse la sorpresa.
El acto de cierre de campaña de este viernes en la Caja Mágica de Madrid vino a confirmar esa creencia. En el mismo recinto en el que 48 horas antes pinchaba el PP de Feijóo, Almeida y Ayuso (no lograron completar el aforo y se quedaron muchos asientos vacíos), el PSOE consiguió un llenazo que superó incluso las expectativas iniciales, con más de 13.000 personas, y tuvieron que retirarse lonas de algunas de las gradas para dar cabida a más militantes. Una muestra de músculo de partido que en Ferraz creen que tendrá correlación con una “histórica” movilización de la izquierda.
“Esta movilización no es habitual y solo hay que comparar nuestra propia campaña de 2023. Entonces calculamos que asistieron a los mítines unas 17.000 personas en total, esta vez estamos muy por encima de 80.000. Y eso no es casualidad ni que hayamos hecho cosas muy diferentes. Es que hay mucha gente de izquierdas movilizada de verdad y que en el ánimo general está la remontada”, explican en el equipo del presidente, donde dan por sentando que en las últimas semanas se ha achicado la brecha entre los bloques de izquierda y de derecha y que la hipótesis de la reedición de un Gobierno de Sánchez no es, aseguran, descabellada.
La foto que trasladan los últimos sondeos diarios que manejan en Ferraz es la del PSOE como primera fuerza política, por encima de 30% del voto y a unos tres puntos de distancia del PP. Y en la suma de los bloques la mayoría absoluta de las derechas no estaría garantizada. Un escenario que el propio Pedro Sánchez define como otra oportunidad para reeditar la remontada de 2023. “¿Pero cómo no van a estar de los nervios con este llenazo? Frente a la involución que representan Feijóo y Abascal, movilización, movilización y movilización. Claro que sí se puede, ¡lo vamos a volver a lograr!, dijo el candidato en la Caja Mágica.
Desde que Sánchez anunciara su decisión de disolver las Cortes el pasado 5 de octubre para convocar elecciones generales anticipadas, muchas cosas han pasado en la política española, en el Gobierno y en el PSOE. Algunas, tan traumáticas como la tragedia ferroviaria de Urda, la segunda en diez meses en la línea Sur de la Alta Velocidad y en la que perdieron la vida 69 personas. Las consecuencias políticas de ese accidente se cobraron, además, la dimisión de Óscar Puente como ministro de Transportes, uno de los escuderos más cercanos al presidente.
Aquella precampaña electoral que arrancó en el contexto de la crisis de vivienda, el desahucio de Maricarmen Abascal y las acampadas por todo el país, evolucionó entonces hacia un contexto mucho menos favorable para los intereses electorales de Pedro Sánchez con la crisis ferroviaria. Pero, contra todo pronóstico, el PSOE consiguió volver a levantar el ánimo. El éxito de las movilizaciones de la huelga general del 11 de noviembre insufló a las izquierdas un espíritu renovado de remontada alimentado, además, por algunos tropiezos de PP y Vox. Y creen en las filas socialistas que el error no forzado de Sánchez del primer debate 'cara a cara' con Feijóo quedó ampliamente subsanado con el discurrir del de este jueves, a cuatro, en el que el líder del PSOE escenificó un tándem a la ofensiva junto a Ada Colau que logró imponerse a Feijóo y Abascal.
El Frente Amplio, a por el 10%
También el Frente Amplio ha apurado los últimos días de la campaña electoral apelando al mantra de la “remontada”, pese a que las encuestas publicadas mostraban a la alianza de izquierdas estancada. No obstante, el papel desempeñado en los debates televisados por su número uno por Madrid, Emilio Delgado, y su candidata, Ada Colau —especialmente esta última— ha inyectado moral a la coalición, que conforme ha avanzado la campaña ha endurecido el tono contra el PSOE para defenderse de su llamada al voto útil.
Esa ilusión se dejó notar en el multitudinario acto de cierre de campaña que celebró este viernes el Frente Amplio en el barrio madrileño de Villaverde. Tras una campaña con mítines de menor formato, la alianza desbordó el espacio La Nave entre gritos de “Ada Ada Ada, Ada remontada” y con un “sí se puede” de reminiscencias moradas: no solo reunió a 4.000 personas en el interior, sino que fuentes de la organización cifraban en otros 2.000 los simpatizantes que se quedaron fuera en una larga cola que daba la vuelta al recinto.
A lo largo de la campaña, los de Colau se han mostrado críticos con el PSOE por asumir ahora propuestas que ha rechazado durante la legislatura. “Si nos vais a copiar las propuestas, dos cosas, copinádnoslas mejor y copiádnoslas antes”, ironizó este viernes la líder de Más Madrid, Mónica García, en el mitin de cierre. No obstante, el Frente Amplio no se toma la estrategia socialista a broma, ya que la alianza considera que tratar de pescar entre su electorado solo puede conducir a que el bloque progresista en su conjunto no tenga opciones de disputar el Gobierno.
En la misma línea se expresaba hace unos días Delgado en una entrevista en elDiario.es. “Creo que hay gente en el PSOE que cree que es más importante tener un buen resultado como partido que ganar las elecciones, y me parece un error”, afirmó el dirigente. Delgado es una de las figuras que el Frente Amplio ha decidido proyectar en la última semana: desde el inicio de la campaña, el número uno por Madrid ha hecho tándem con Colau como los dos principales candidatos de la alianza, pero en los últimos días también ha sido el protagonista de varios vídeos, uno de los cuales le muestra practicando deportes de contacto.
Con él, explican fuentes del Frente Amplio, la alianza ha querido conectar con sectores en los que otros perfiles tienen menos tirón. No obstante, la coalición da por hecho que empeorará el resultado obtenido en 2023, cuando Sumar —entonces con Podemos dentro— logró 31 diputados. Pero la obsesión del Frente Amplio, repetida hasta la saciedad en mítines, entrevistas e intervenciones, es la de alcanzar al menos el 10% de los sufragios, la barrera que permite sortear los efectos más perniciosos del sistema electoral. Especialmente cuando en algunos de sus caladeros habituales de voto la alianza tendrá que enfrentarse a rivales de ámbito territorial muy fuertes, como Adelante Andalucía o ERC.
Irene Montero se la juega
El desempeño en las urnas de esos partidos del bloque progresista que no son el PSOE ni el Frente Amplio es también fundamental para una hipotética suma de 176 diputados que permitiría la investidura de Pedro Sánchez. Además de los mencionados, cada escaño será fundamental: los del BNG, EH Bildu, el PNV y, llegado el caso, Coalición Canaria, quien ha negado que vaya a dar su voto al PP si va de la mano de Vox
En esas cuentas también podría estar Podemos, cuya campaña se ha centrado casi en exclusiva en el perfil de su candidata, Irene Montero. Tanto que las siglas del partido han sido relegadas casi hasta desaparecer de la cartelería de los morados en favor del nombre de la dirigente.
Sus perspectivas son poco halagüeñas, y Podemos no ha logrado dar la vuelta a las encuestas conforme se acercan las elecciones. Todo lo contrario: la media de los sondeos del pasado lunes les situaba en apenas un 1,3% de los votos.
Podemos tienen opciones de obtener escaños en Alicante y Barcelona, aunque no con su marca, sino dentro de las listas de ERC en Catalunya y formando parte de la coalición Compromís-Front Valenciá en la Comunitat. Mucho más en el aire queda el regreso de Irene Montero al Congreso por Madrid, si bien Podemos ha optado por desdeñar las encuestas que apuntan a la posibilidad de quedarse sin representación en esa circunscripción. Desde el partido apuntan a que no solo el escaño de Montero está asegurado, sino que está pugnando por conseguir un segundo.
En la estrategia de Podemos ha sido fundamental la figura del candidato de ERC, Gabriel Rufián, con quien Montero cerró una alianza política y electoral, y que ha protagonizado los actos más multitudinarios de una campaña en la que los morados han tratado de mantener su espacio en la izquierda caricaturizando a PSOE y Frente Amplio como dos caras de un mismo proyecto.
El partido se ha quejado, igualmente, de que no se le haya invitado a participar en los debates electorales de esta semana: el del lunes, que reunía a los partidos con grupo parlamentario —Podemos no lo ha tenido esta legislatura— y el del jueves, en el que participaron las cuatro principales candidaturas de ámbito nacional.
Para todos y todas, el domingo llegará el veredicto de las urnas, que da o quita razones de forma definitiva.

noticias.titulo: Cazorla en un fin de semana: castillos, patrimonio y rutas por una de las sierras más espectaculares de Jaén
noticias.resumen: Del castillo de la Yedra a la Cerrada de Elías, recorremos Cazorla y algunos de los rincones más interesantes de su parque natural en una escapada de tres días entre cultura, historia y naturaleza Mucho más que un castillo: siete pueblos españoles que nacieron al amparo de una fortaleza Cazorla tiene una particularidad a tener muy en cuenta en esta época del año: aquí el pueblo y la montaña forman parte del mismo plan. noticias.texto:
Cazorla en un fin de semana: castillos, patrimonio y rutas por una de las sierras más espectaculares de Jaén
Cazorla tiene una particularidad a tener muy en cuenta en esta época del año: aquí el pueblo y la montaña forman parte del mismo plan. Basta con recorrer unos kilómetros para pasar de las calles empedradas, los castillos y las plazas de su casco histórico a los bosques, ríos y senderos del Parque Natural de las Sierras de Cazorla, Segura y Las Villas.
Estamos en uno de los espacios naturales protegidos más extensos de España, con más de 200.000 hectáreas de montañas, bosques, ríos, barrancos y embalses. Por aquí discurre buena parte del curso alto del Guadalquivir, que nace en estas sierras, y habitan especies como ciervos, cabras montesas y numerosas aves rapaces. Hay mucho terreno por recorrer, pero no hace falta alejarse demasiado de Cazorla para empezar a disfrutarlo.
